title: Parents and carers of under-18s
intro: If your child or teenager has told you they are trans, non-binary or questioning their gender, this page covers what helps first, how care works in South Australia, who gives consent, and where to get support. It is general information, not advice about your child.

list: **Listen.** Thank them for telling you; it often takes courage. Listen more than you talk.
**Use their name and pronouns if they ask.** Mistakes happen. Correct yourself and keep going.
**You do not need all the answers.** It is fine to say, "I love you, and I want to understand."
**Let them lead on who else is told.** Ask who already knows and who they want to tell.
**Look after yourself too.** Many parents feel worried, sad or relieved, sometimes all at once. Other parents can help (see the support list below).

sections.h: Does every young person want medical treatment?
body: No. Exploring gender looks different for everyone. Some young people change their name, clothes or hair; some change nothing on the outside for a while. Feelings can stay the same or change over time.
Only some young people who get gender-affirming care go on to use puberty blockers or hormones [1]. Support at home and at school helps whatever path your child takes.

sections.h: How does care for under-18s work in South Australia?
body: The public specialist service is the **Gender Diversity Service at the Women's and Children's Hospital (WCH)** in North Adelaide. It sees children and young people up to 17 years old from anywhere in South Australia [2]. Its care follows the SA Statewide Gender Diversity Model of Care, the Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents, and South Australia's consent law [2, 3, 4].

**Getting a referral.** The service needs a written referral from a GP, paediatrician, psychiatrist, psychologist or other mental health professional, saying who to contact for appointments (your child or you) [2]. Your GP is usually the easiest start. The [Trans Health SA directory](https://transhealthsa.com/directory/) lists affirming GPs.
**Waiting.** Demand is high, so there is usually a wait for the first appointment. Keep seeing your GP, or whoever referred you, while you wait [2].
list: **Step 1.** A "get to know you" appointment with a mental health clinician. If your child is under 16, a parent or legal guardian must know about it and come too.
**Step 2.** A mental health opinion, often over several appointments. Every young person sees the team's psychiatrist before any referral to the medical team.

**Step 3.** Appointments with a fertility counselling specialist and a paediatrician or paediatric endocrinologist. Medicines are not started at the first medical appointment. Blood tests, a bone density scan and height, weight and blood pressure checks may come first.
**Step 4.** If treatment starts, there are regular check-ups. The team works with your GP, who may give injections closer to home. The hospital school can also help with school concerns.
sections.note: An August 2026 review found the service's practice in line with the Statewide Model of Care and recommended seven improvements, including a clearer move to adult care at 18 [2, 5].

list: **16 and over:** a young person aged 16 or over can make decisions about their own medical treatment as validly as an adult.

**Under 16:** a doctor may treat a child if a parent or guardian consents. A child's own consent is enough only if the doctor believes the child understands the nature, consequences and risks and that the treatment is in their best interests, and a second doctor who examines the child before treatment starts agrees in writing.
after: At the WCH service, a parent or legal guardian must consent before medical treatment starts for anyone under 16 [2]. In practice, families are usually involved at every step. Rules for under-18s differ between states [7, p9].

sections.h: What is happening with puberty blockers in Australia?
body: Puberty blockers (GnRH analogues) pause the changes of puberty. The WCH service describes this as "reversible pubertal suppression" [2]. They can affect bone density while they are used, so bone scans are part of the checks [2, 4]. The [GnRH analogues page](/medicines/gnrh-analogues) explains how they work and their side effects. Reviews of the research, including the University of York systematic review done for the Cass Review in 2024, found that blockers reliably pause puberty and can lower bone density while they are used, but that there is not yet good-quality evidence about their longer-term effects on wellbeing [8, 9].
list: **National guidelines.** On 31 January 2025 the federal Health Minister asked the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) to write new national guidelines for under-18s with gender dysphoria [10]. Interim advice on puberty blockers is due for public comment in late 2026 (November to December on NHMRC's timeline); the full guidelines will take about three years [10]. It had not been published by 8 November 2026.

**Queensland.** Queensland public hospitals have paused starting puberty blockers and hormones for under-18s with gender dysphoria. On 19 December 2025 the Queensland Government said the pause will continue until the results of a UK trial (PATHWAYS) are known, expected in 2031 [11].
**South Australia.** The WCH service continues to offer puberty blockers and hormones to young people who are assessed as suitable [2].
**Cost.** The WCH pharmacy charges a gap payment for the medicine [2]. No puberty blocker is PBS-subsidised for this use (see [Costs](#/costs)).
sections.note: This is changing, so ask your GP or the WCH team about the latest.

list: [Kids Helpline](https://kidshelpline.com.au/): 1800 55 1800, free, 24 hours, ages 5 to 25 [12]
[headspace](https://headspace.org.au/): mental health support for ages 12 to 25; phone 1800 650 890, online chat 3pm to 10pm [13, 14]
[QLife](https://qlife.org.au/): 1800 184 527, LGBTIQ+ peer support for young people and families, 3pm to 9pm every day [15]
[Minus18](https://www.minus18.org.au/): Australia's charity for LGBTQIA+ young people
[13YARN](https://www.13yarn.org.au/): 13 92 76, 24 hours, crisis support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people [16]
[Transcend Australia](https://transcend.org.au/): support for families of trans and gender diverse children
[PFLAG+ Australia](https://pflagaustralia.org.au/): peer support for parents, carers and friends
[Parents of Gender Diverse Children: South Australia](https://pgdc.org.au/resources/south-australia)
[Trans Health SA: for parents](https://transhealthsa.com/for-parents/)
[TransHub: for allies and families](https://www.transhub.org.au/allies)
[Lifeline](https://www.lifeline.org.au/): 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14, 24 hours [17]

sections.h: When should I get help straight away?
body: Call **000** if your child's life is in danger, or if they have hurt themselves or have a plan to.
list: **Under 16:** call 000, go to the nearest emergency department or the WCH Emergency Department, or ask for the WCH 24-hour Emergency Mental Health Nurse through the hospital switchboard on (08) 8161 7000 [2].
**16 and 17:** go to the nearest emergency department or the Urgent Mental Health Care Centre (215 Grenfell Street, Adelaide), or call the Mental Health Triage Service on 13 14 65 [2].
The WCH gender team does not provide crisis support [2].
